summary: Defines MIB objects for managing SONET/SDH interfaces. It is a companion to the documents that define managed objects for the other interface types. It is a draft standard.

plainLanguage.summary: This document defines the standard SNMP objects for monitoring SONET and SDH optical circuits. A manager reads them to see whether a line is healthy, which faults have appeared, and how many errored seconds each layer has recorded over the last quarter of an hour.

questions: how does snmp monitor sonet interfaces
subtitle: The SNMP objects a manager reads to see how a SONET or SDH optical line is performing.

tldr.problem: Optical lines fail in many different ways, and a network manager needs the same view of those faults whatever vendor built the equipment.
tldr.mechanism: The document defines a MIB module with one table per layer of the SONET or SDH hierarchy. Each table reports the current status, the counters for the current interval and a history of 15-minute intervals, using the fault and error definitions from the SONET and SDH standards.
tldr.outcome: A manager can read the same objects for a section, line, path or virtual tributary, and can tell a momentary glitch from a fault that has lasted long enough to take the circuit out of service. The document replaced RFC 2558 in 2003.

today: RFC 3592 is a Draft Standard on the IETF Standards Track. It replaced RFC 2558 in 2003, which had itself replaced RFC 1595, and it has not itself been obsoleted or updated. It uses the textual conventions for 15-minute performance history defined in RFC 3593.

sections.title: What the MIB Covers
sections.content:
The memo defines a MIB module for use with network management protocols in TCP/IP-based internets, and in particular for managing SONET/SDH interfaces. It is a companion to the documents that define the managed objects for the DS1/E1/DS2/E2 and DS3/E3 interface types.

The objects apply when the media used to realise an interface is a SONET/SDH interface, which is the case for three values of the ifType variable in the Internet-standard MIB: sonet (39), sonetPath (50) and sonetVT (51). The definitions are based on the SONET/SDH specifications in ANSI T1.105 and T1.106-1988 and on CCITT G.707, G.708, G.709 and G.783.

Managed objects are reached through the Management Information Base and accessed with SNMP, and they are defined with the mechanisms of the Structure of Management Information. This module complies with SMIv2, and the textual conventions it uses are defined in RFC 2579 and in RFC 3593.
sections.plainLanguage: The document covers three kinds of optical interface: the physical line itself, the paths carried on it and the small tributary signals carried on those paths. Every manager can then read the same objects whatever equipment is in the path.

sections.title: Layers as Interfaces
sections.content:
SONET/SDH supports several levels of multiplexing. In SONET, an STS-3 has three SONET Paths while an STS-3c has one, and an STS-12 can have four STS-3c paths. A SONET Synchronous Payload Envelope can carry many Virtual Tributaries, for example 28 VT1.5s in one envelope. An SPE and a VT in SONET are collectively called a Virtual Container in SDH, and an STS is called a Synchronous Transport Module in SDH.

Not all equipment terminates all layers. A regenerator terminates Sections only and is transparent above that, while add-drop multiplexers and digital cross-connect systems terminate Lines. Terminal multiplexers may also terminate Paths and VTs. The MIB II system group and interfaces group handle this by representing each SONET/SDH layer that the equipment terminates as an ifEntry. The exact configuration and multiplexing of the layers is held in the ifStackTable and the ifInvStackTable.

For the combined medium, section and line layer, only the ifGeneralInformationGroup needs to be supported. The ifType is sonet(39), ifSpeed is the line rate in bits per second, for example 155520000 bps, and ifPhysAddress holds the Circuit Identifier. For Paths the ifType is sonetPath(50), with a path rate of 50112000 bps for an STS-1 path, and for VTs the ifType is sonetVT(51), with 1728000 bps for a VT1.5.
sections.plainLanguage: Each layer that a piece of equipment actually terminates becomes one row in the generic interface table. A regenerator stops at the section layer, a switch stops at the line, and a multiplexer may stop at paths and tributaries as well.

sections.title: The Groups and Their Tables
sections.content:
The module is organised into groups that mirror the layer hierarchy. The SONET/SDH Medium Group holds the configuration of the interface itself, with objects for the medium type, the line coding, the line type, the circuit identifier, a loopback configuration and the interval bookkeeping. The Section Group and the Line Group each hold a Current group and an Interval group. The Far End Line Group, the Path Group, the Far End Path Group, the Virtual Tributary Group and the Far End VT Group follow the same pattern, and each of them has a Current group and an Interval group of its own.

The Current tables report what is happening now, using the PerfCurrentCount textual convention, and the Interval tables keep the history in 15-minute buckets, using PerfIntervalCount. The medium group records how many previous 15-minute intervals hold data: an interface must be able to support at least 4, the default is 32, and the maximum is 96. The object sonetMediumTimeElapsed counts the seconds since the current measurement period began, up to 900, which is one 15-minute interval.
sections.plainLanguage: Every layer gets the same shape: a table for what is happening right now, and a table that keeps the last day and a half in quarter-hour slots. The far-end tables report what the other end of the circuit sees.

sections.title: The Faults the Equipment Reports
sections.content:
The fault names come from the SONET standard T1.231 for SONET circuits and from CCITT G.783 for SDH circuits, and only the SONET performance monitoring terminology is defined in this document. A Loss of Signal defect is declared when no transitions are detected on the incoming signal before descrambling, after 2.3 to 100 microseconds without transitions, and cleared after a 125 microsecond interval. A Loss of Frame defect is declared when an out of frame defect persists for 3 milliseconds, and an out of frame event is the occurrence of four contiguous errored frame alignment words, terminated when two contiguous error-free frame words are detected. A Loss of Pointer defect is declared when a valid pointer is missing for eight consecutive frames.

An Alarm Indication Signal is a downstream alarm: a line AIS is a "111" pattern in the K2 byte, an STS-Path AIS is all ones in the H1 and H2 bytes, and a VT-Path AIS applies only to floating VTs. A Remote Defect Indication, also called a far end error, tells the near end that a fault was found further along. The status objects report these conditions as a bit map, so several can be signalled at once: the path status uses bit 1 for no defect, 2 for STS-Path loss of pointer, 4 for STS-Path AIS, 8 for STS-Path RDI, 16 for unequipped and 32 for a signal label mismatch. A Coding Violation is a bit interleaved parity error, counted with BIP-8 in the B1 byte for sections, BIP-8 in the B2 bytes for lines, BIP-8 in the B3 byte for paths and BIP-2 in the V5 byte for floating virtual tributaries.
sections.plainLanguage: Optical faults come in named kinds: no signal, lost framing, a lost pointer, an alarm sent downstream, and a report of a fault at the far end. Each layer reports which of them it sees as a set of bits, so several can be true at once.

sections.title: How the Counters Are Counted
sections.content:
An Errored Second is a second with one or more coding violations at that layer, or with one or more incoming defects such as a severely errored frame, loss of signal, alarm indication signal or loss of pointer. A Severely Errored Second is a second with a large number of coding violations at that layer, or a second in which at least one incoming defect occurred. A Severely Errored Framing Second is a second containing one or more severely errored frame events, and is counted only at the section layer.

At the line, path and VT layers the interface is said to be unavailable at the onset of 10 contiguous severely errored seconds, and those 10 seconds count as unavailable time. It becomes available again at the onset of 10 contiguous seconds with no severely errored seconds, and those 10 seconds are excluded from unavailable time. While the interface is unavailable, the only counter that moves is the unavailable seconds count at that layer; all the others are frozen.

Because the signal state lags the data by ten seconds, an implementation that updates its counters in real time must be ready to correct them afterwards, and the document explains two ways of doing this. Appendix A describes a delay-line approach in which the one-second statistics are held for ten seconds before any counter is updated. The document also defines the object sonetSESthresholdSet, which records which set of thresholds is in use, because the standards changed the threshold values over time; if the object is not implemented, the thresholds of RFC 1595 apply. Changing the value invalidates all the severely errored second statistics collected before the change.
sections.plainLanguage: Two seconds in a row with serious errors put the circuit into unavailable time, and it takes ten clean seconds to bring it back. Counting that exactly is awkward, because the equipment learns about a fault ten seconds late, so the counters are either delayed or corrected afterwards.

sections.title: Configuring the Medium
sections.content:
The medium table holds the objects a manager can change to describe and provision the interface. sonetMediumType says whether a SONET or an SDH signal is used across the interface. sonetMediumLineCoding describes the line coding: B3ZS and CMI are used for electrical SONET/SDH signals, and Non-Return to Zero and Return to Zero for optical ones. sonetMediumLineType describes the physical medium, from short or long range single-mode fibre and multi-mode fibre to coax and unshielded twisted pair for electrical interfaces, with a value for anything else.

sonetMediumCircuitIdentifier holds the transmission vendor's own circuit identifier, which is useful when talking to the vendor during troubleshooting, and sonetMediumLoopbackConfig enables or disables loopback configurations. The interval bookkeeping is completed by sonetMediumInvalidIntervals, which counts the missing intervals where data could not be collected, for example where the agent is a proxy. The width of a path is also writable, through sonetPathCurrentWidth, whose values run from sts1(1) and sts3cSTM1(2) through sts192cSTM64(6) to sts768cSTM256(7).
sections.plainLanguage: These are the settings a manager can change on the physical side of the circuit: whether it is SONET or SDH, what line coding and fibre it uses, and the vendor's own reference for the circuit.

sections.title: What Changed from RFC 2558
sections.content:
The module's revision clause lists what changed since RFC 2558. A typographical error in the sonetSESthresholdSet enumeration was corrected, support for sts192cSTM64(6) and sts768cSTM256(7) was added to sonetPathCurrentWidth, the description of the applicability of VTs for SDH was corrected, a clarification was added that coding violation counts should be frozen during severely errored seconds, and two further typographical errors were fixed.

The revision clause also records the longer history. The RFC 1595 version of this module updated the module identity, used the PerfCurrentCount and PerfIntervalCount textual conventions in place of Gauge32 where applicable, gave the agent the option of delaying updates to performance counts instead of adjusting them retroactively, made the formerly read-only medium objects read-write so that circuits can be provisioned, added the invalid-interval count and the loopback configuration object, added the threshold set object, and added a validity column to each interval table.
sections.plainLanguage: The 2003 version fixes a handful of errors and adds two higher path rates. The list of changes from the very first version shows how the module grew into something a provisioning tool can use.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A number of objects in this module have a MAX-ACCESS clause of read-write: sonetMediumType, sonetMediumLineCoding, sonetMediumLineType, sonetMediumCircuitIdentifier, sonetMediumLoopbackConfig, sonetSESthresholdSet, sonetPathCurrentWidth and sonetVTCurrentWidth. Writes to these can be disruptive, ranging from invalid performance data to traffic interruptions, so supporting SET operations in a non-secure environment without proper protection can have a negative effect on network operations.

The readable objects may also be considered sensitive, since collectively they give extensive information about the performance of interfaces and can reveal aspects of their configuration. In such environments it is important to control even read and notification access, and possibly to encrypt the values when sending them over the network with SNMP. SNMP versions before SNMPv3 did not include adequate security, and even on a secure network there is no control over who may read or change the objects.

The document recommends the security features of the SNMPv3 framework, including full support for its cryptographic mechanisms for authentication and privacy, and says that deploying versions before SNMPv3 is not recommended. It is then the responsibility of the operator to configure the SNMP entity so that only principals with legitimate rights can read or change the objects.
sections.plainLanguage: Some of these objects can change how the circuit behaves, so writing them carelessly can interrupt traffic. The document says to use SNMPv3 with its encryption, and to keep the readings themselves to authorised users.

items.title: Loss of Signal
items.text: No transitions on the incoming signal, detected after 2.3 to 100 microseconds.

items.title: Loss of Frame
items.text: Four contiguous errored frame alignment words. The defect is declared after 3 milliseconds.

items.title: Loss of Pointer
items.text: No valid pointer for eight consecutive frames.

items.title: Alarm Indication Signal
items.text: A downstream alarm raised when a lower layer has failed.

items.title: Remote Defect Indication
items.text: The far end reporting that it has found a fault further along.

items.title: Coding Violation
items.text: A bit interleaved parity error, counted with the BIP checks of the layer.

items.label: sonetPathNoDefect
items.desc: Set if and only if no other flag is set.

items.label: sonetPathSignalLabelMismatch
items.desc: The received signal label does not match the provisioned one.

items.title: Errored Second
items.text: A second with one or more coding violations, or with an incoming defect.

items.title: Severely Errored Second
items.text: A second with a large number of coding violations, or with an incoming defect.

items.title: Severely Errored Framing Second
items.text: A second containing one or more severely errored frame events. Counted at the section layer only.

items.title: Unavailable Second
items.text: The interface is unavailable from the onset of 10 contiguous severely errored seconds, and available again after 10 contiguous clean seconds.
